blocks.text: PEFT is the Hugging Face library that implements the parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques, LoRA, QLoRA, and related methods, all covered conceptually in earlier modules of this course, providing ready to use code so you do not need to implement the underlying adapter math yourself.
This topic covers how the library wraps a base model with trainable adapters, how adapter checkpoints work, and the practical workflow for training and later merging or swapping adapters.
1. PEFT the Concept vs PEFT the Library

blocks.alt: PEFT concepts like LoRA and QLoRA are distinct from the PEFT library implementation

blocks.text: It is worth distinguishing parameter-efficient fine-tuning as a general concept, covered in an earlier module, from the PEFT library specifically, the Hugging Face package that provides tested, ready to use implementations of LoRA, QLoRA, and other adapter-based methods on top of Transformers models, covered in the previous topic.
2. Wrapping a Base Model With Adapters

blocks.alt: A base model is passed through get_peft_model, producing a wrapped model with adapters

blocks.text: The get_peft_model function takes an already loaded base model and a configuration object, then returns a wrapped version of that model with adapter layers inserted at the specified locations, ready for training exactly like any other Transformers model.

code.content:
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

config = LoraConfig(
    r=8,
    lora_alpha=16,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"],
    lora_dropout=0.05,
)
peft_model = get_peft_model(base_model, config)
peft_model.print_trainable_parameters()

blocks.text: 3. Configuring LoRA Through LoraConfig

blocks.alt: LoraConfig sets rank, alpha, and target modules

blocks.text: The LoraConfig object exposes the key hyperparameters covered conceptually in the earlier LoRA and rank topics, r for adapter rank, lora_alpha for scaling, and target_modules specifying exactly which layers, typically attention projection matrices, get adapters attached, giving direct control over the LoRA setup through simple configuration rather than custom code.
4. Frozen Base Weights, Trainable Adapters

blocks.alt: Full model weights stay frozen while small adapter weights remain trainable

blocks.text: Once wrapped, the library automatically freezes the base model original weights and marks only the newly inserted adapter parameters as trainable, exactly implementing the frozen-base, trainable-adapter split that makes parameter-efficient fine-tuning memory efficient in the first place.

blocks.text: 5. Small, Portable Adapter Checkpoints

blocks.alt: A trained adapter is saved on its own, producing a small checkpoint file

blocks.text: Because only the adapter weights were actually trained, saving a PEFT checkpoint only needs to store those adapter parameters, typically a tiny fraction of the full model size, producing checkpoint files that are dramatically smaller and faster to share than a full fine-tuned model would be.

blocks.title: This portability is a major practical advantage
blocks.content: A LoRA adapter for a large model can often be just a few megabytes, compared to gigabytes for the full model, making it practical to store and distribute many task-specific adapters cheaply.

blocks.text: 6. One Base Model, Many Adapters

blocks.alt: One base model supports separate adapters for task A, task B, and task C

blocks.text: Because adapters are small and separate from the frozen base model, a single deployed base model can be paired with different task-specific adapters loaded on demand, letting one underlying model effectively serve many different fine-tuned behaviors without duplicating the full model weights for each.
7. Merging Adapters Back Into the Base Model

blocks.alt: Adapter weights go through merge_and_unload, producing a merged standalone model

blocks.text: When adapter-swapping flexibility is not needed and a single self contained model is preferred, the library merge_and_unload method mathematically folds the adapter weights back into the base model weights, producing a standalone model that behaves identically to the adapted version but no longer needs the PEFT wrapping at inference time.
8. Beyond LoRA: Other Supported Methods

The library also implements other parameter-efficient techniques beyond LoRA, prompt tuning and prefix tuning among them, both covered conceptually in an earlier module, following the same general pattern of a configuration object and get_peft_model wrapping, making it straightforward to experiment with different adapter methods using largely the same code.
9. PEFT Library Within a Fine-Tuning Pipeline

PEFT typically works alongside the Trainer API from Transformers, covered in the previous topic, and often alongside Accelerate for distributed training, covered in the next topic, the wrapped PEFT model behaves like a normal Transformers model for training purposes, so the rest of a fine-tuning pipeline usually needs little to no modification.
Worked Example

A team wants to fine-tune the same base model for three different internal tools, a code assistant, a documentation writer, and a support bot. Using the PEFT library, they train three separate LoRA adapters against the same frozen base model, each only a few megabytes.

In production, they load whichever adapter matches the current request on top of a single shared base model instance, avoiding the cost of hosting three separate full fine-tuned models while still getting task-specific behavior for each use case.
Common Mistakes

items: Setting target_modules to layers that do not actually benefit from adaptation, wasting adapter capacity
Forgetting to call print_trainable_parameters to sanity check that the base model is actually frozen as expected
Merging an adapter into the base model too early, losing the flexibility to swap or update it later
Not realizing multiple adapters can share one base model, and unnecessarily duplicating full models per task instead

Sketch a LoraConfig for fine-tuning a model on a new task, choosing a rank and target_modules value, then explain, using the frozen-versus-trainable split covered in this topic, roughly how much smaller you would expect the resulting adapter checkpoint to be compared to the full model.
Key Takeaway

The PEFT library provides ready to use implementations of LoRA and related adapter-based techniques on top of Transformers models, wrapping a base model with small trainable adapters through get_peft_model, producing compact, portable checkpoints that can be merged into a standalone model or kept separate to support many task-specific adapters on one shared base model.
